label: Public money: what it costs those who pay (ours)

rows.label: Marginal cost of public funds: what a dollar of public money costs those who pay, in dollars

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on Dahlby (2008), The Marginal Cost of Public Funds: Theory and Applications (MIT Press), and Auriol and Warlters (2012), Journal of Development Economics
source.note: One figure for every model that counts the cost of public money to those who pay it (taxpayers, or other public spending given up).

rows.explainer: Raising a dollar of tax costs the economy more than a dollar, through the work and spending it discourages: estimates for rich countries' taxes run from about 1.1 to 1.5 (Dahlby 2008), and for African countries' taxes mostly 1.1 to 1.3 (Auriol and Warlters 2012, 38 countries). 1.2, range 1 (money shifted from other spending) to 1.5.

rows.label: How US federal taxes fall, relative to a tax proportional to consumption
rows.explainer: On the log-income scale a dollar taken from someone costs 1 over their consumption; a tax proportional to consumption costs 1 over the national-accounts mean (a multiple of 1), a progressive one less (above 1). Federal programmes are paid for by the federal income tax and borrowing, which fall mostly on richer households: 1.4, range 1 (borrowing repaid by everyone alike) to 2. Read by every model that values federal money net of what it costs those who pay; state and local money (regressive sales taxes) takes its own figure.

rows.label: How US state and local taxes fall, relative to a tax proportional to consumption
rows.explainer: On the log scale a dollar taken from someone costs 1 over their consumption, so a tax proportional to true consumption costs 1 over the national-accounts mean (a multiple of 1); a progressive tax costs less (above 1), a regressive one more (below 1). ITEP's Who Pays (7th edition, 2024) finds state and local taxes regressive against income (11.4% of income for the poorest fifth, 7.2% for the top 1%), but close to proportional against consumption, since poorer households consume more than their income: 1.05, range 0.75 (money taken from other programmes for poorer households, or regressive sales taxes) to 1.6 (income-tax money). Read by every model that values state or local money net of what it costs those who pay (Habitat for Humanity's advocacy, Prison Policy Initiative's free-call laws and jail commissions).
